To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the effect of an infectious disease on population growth is not necessarily monotonic, and that bistable behaviour is a generic outcome of the interaction between the disease and the population.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the effects of infectious disease on population growth are extremely complex, and the precise outcome depends critically on a number of parameters, some of which are difficult or impossible to estimate.
the effect of a macroparasitic disease on the growth rate of a population can be either positive, negative or neutral, depending on the parameter values.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the population growth of the host species can be either accelerated or decelerated by the disease, depending on the parameter values, and that in the latter case the growth may be oscillatory.
the population growth rate can be reduced to zero by the disease for a certain range of parameter values.
for a wide class of diseases, the growth of the population is either exponential or periodic, and never linear.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effect of an infectious disease on the population growth rate is not necessarily negative, even if the disease has a negative impact on the individual fitness.
a simple bifurcation analysis can be used to understand how the effect of an infectious disease on population growth can be either positive or negative, depending on the value of a single parameter.
